text: Given a string of just parentheses, square brackets, and curly braces, decide if the brackets are validly matched — same type, correct order, and every closer has an opener.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — open, close, square open, square close, curly open, curly close is true. Open paren then close square is false, wrong type. And open paren, open square, close paren, close square is false — wrong order, even though the counts match. So valid brackets nest properly: the most recently opened one must close first, which is last in, first out. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Right. The length goes up to ten to the fourth.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. This problem reminds me of a stack, because last in, first out is exactly what a stack gives me. Push openers; on a closer, the stack top must be its matching opener — pop if so, else fail. At the end, the stack must be empty. Three checks cover the three ways to fail: a top mismatch, for wrong type or order; an empty stack on a closer, for an extra closer; and a non-empty stack at the end, for an extra opener. That's linear time.

Counting loses order. Open paren, open square, close paren, close square has one of each but is invalid. The stack catches it, because when the close paren arrives, the top is a square bracket, not a paren. Only a stack remembers which opener is currently innermost.

Here's the plan. One: for each character, an opener gets pushed. Two: for a closer, if the stack is empty or the top isn't its matching opener, return false; otherwise pop. Three: return whether the stack is empty. One thing worth flagging — I'll check empty before calling top, to avoid undefined behavior on an empty stack. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. One loop with three closer branches — close paren, close curly, close square — each checking that the stack is non-empty and the top is the matching opener, then popping. Anything else is an opener, so it gets pushed. After the loop, I return whether the stack is empty. One thing worth flagging — the order inside each check, empty first, then top. The or short-circuits, so top is never called on an empty stack.

Let's dry-run the code. Open paren, open square, close square, close paren — expected true. Both closers find their partner on top, so the stack ends empty and I return true. The row that matters is the same brackets reordered: open paren, open square, close paren, close square. When the close paren arrives, the top is a square bracket, so I return false. That matches. Corner cases: a lone close square is false — closer on an empty stack. A lone open paren is false — the stack isn't empty at the end.
The loop only fails on closers. Pure openers, like two open parens, never trigger a failure inside the loop, but they leave items on the stack. The final empty check catches those unclosed openers.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — one pass, with constant-time push, pop, and top. Space is linear in the worst case, when every character is an opener. A single bracket type could use a counter, but multiple types need the stack to remember which opener is innermost. The same stack idea powers evaluating postfix expressions and removing invalid parentheses.
Clean — the last in, first out fit, the three checks, the short-circuit point, and the counting versus stack distinction. Done.
